claims.claim: Early stakeholder identification can reveal the organizations and individuals that may need involvement, as well as the contributions or information a project may need from them.

Stakeholder information can include how a person or group is affected, what information or input is relevant, and the constraints or needs that should be examined; a label alone does not determine whose view prevails.
Needs, expectations, constraints, and interfaces are relevant inputs to requirements work, so overlooking affected users or operators can leave a project with incomplete information.
A project communication approach can identify information content, format, security needs, channels, frequency, and communication responsibilities; the appropriate choices depend on context.

Ethical stakeholder engagement is an educational inference: use stakeholder analysis to understand relevant effects and information needs, communicate honestly and respectfully, and avoid treating people as obstacles to be managed.
Stakeholder analysis is revisable because the project, its effects, and available evidence can change; it does not guarantee consensus or project success.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The sources discuss stakeholder work in particular professional and public-sector systems contexts rather than a universal procedure.
positions: PMI's article describes one initiation and communication approach in an organizational setting.
GAO describes needs, constraints, interfaces, and validation in a systems-management setting.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses their shared, high-level reasoning: find materially affected parties, understand relevant needs and constraints, and adapt communication to context. It does not prescribe a register, authority chain, or engagement tactic.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft could imply that a stakeholder map fixes power relationships, that every stakeholder has the same authority, or that communication is a tool for obtaining agreement.
correctionsNeeded: Defines stakeholder identification as inquiry rather than a contact list or persuasion exercise.
Separates interests, influence, impact, and formal decision authority.
Uses an original accessible transit-alert example while avoiding advice to a real organization.
rightsIssues: PMI's conference paper was read live and is treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; no source prose, figures, or templates were reproduced.
GAO reports are public-domain U.S. government publications; the lesson uses original prose and reproduces no tables or diagrams.

questionKeyCheck.method: Read every saved prompt, all four options, correctIndex, explanation, and sourceIds after writing.
questionKeyCheck.result: Exactly five four-option questions. Keys span A through D, no position is used more than twice, and the bank includes recall, application, and analysis.

sourceRecords.title: How do we start a project? Ensuring the right sponsorship, stakeholder alignment and thoughtful preparation for a project
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports the role of early project purpose, sponsorship, initial information gaps, and stakeholder identification. It is an authored PMI learning-library article rather than a universal rule; original prose only and no templates or wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Air Traffic Control: System Management Capabilities Improved, but More Can Be Done to Institutionalize Improvements
sourceRecords.notes: Read live, especially pages 75–83. Supports the bounded systems example: elicit needs, expectations, constraints, and interfaces; translate them to customer requirements; analyze requirements for necessity and sufficiency; and validate intended-use performance using appropriate techniques. Original prose only; no federal procedure is presented as universal.

sourceRecords.title: Information Technology: Education Needs to Address Student Aid Modernization Weaknesses (GAO-23-105333)
sourceRecords.notes: Official GAO report checked live. Supports general descriptions of defining, validating, controlling, and tracking baseline requirements; used only for original synthesis.
